key_terms.meaning: The inclined tensile stress produced by shear; the beam cracks where it exceeds the tensile strength of concrete.
Largest tensile stress at a point, σ₁ = (σ_x+σ_y)/2 + √[((σ_x−σ_y)/2)² + τ²]; a shear crack opens where σ₁ exceeds the concrete tensile strength.
Shear carried across a crack by friction between the rough, interlocking faces of broken aggregate.
Shear carried by the steel bars crossing a crack, which resist sliding of the two faces like small dowels.
The section at distance d from the face of the support where the design shear is taken, d being the effective depth in mm.
τ_v = V_u/(b d), with V_u the factored shear in N, b the web width in mm, d the effective depth in mm.

key_terms.term: Design shear strength of concrete τ_c
key_terms.meaning: Shear stress the concrete alone carries, read from the code table against p_t = 100 A_st/(b d).
Upper limit of shear stress for the section; above it the section must be enlarged, because stirrups cannot help.
Closed links carrying shear, with V_us = 0.87 f_y A_sv d / s_v, where A_sv is the leg area in mm², f_y in N/mm², s_v the spacing in mm.
Shear steel at angle α to the axis, contributing V_us = 0.87 f_y A_sv d (sin α + cos α)/s_v.
A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y); links are required even when τ_v < τ_c.
V_e = V_u + 1.6 T_u/b, the shear used for design when a torque T_u also acts.
M_t = T_u (1 + D/b)/1.7, with D the overall depth in mm and b the width in mm.
Shear stress at the steel–concrete interface, τ_bd = F/(π φ L), with F the bar force in N, φ the bar diameter in mm, L the embedment in mm.
L_d = φ σ_s/(4 τ_bd), the embedment needed to develop bar stress σ_s without pull-out.
4φ for each 45° of bend, with a maximum of 16φ for a standard hook.
Point on the span where a bar is no longer needed for bending; the bar must continue past it by at least d or 12φ, whichever is greater.
Overlap of two bars that passes force from one to the other; the lap length is at least the development length.
Distance from the outer concrete surface to the nearest surface of the reinforcement, used for durability and fire checks.
Cover value written on the drawing and adopted in design, never less than the code minimum for the exposure class.

takeaways: Shear cracks are diagonal tension cracks; the beam survives them through concrete in compression, aggregate interlock, dowel action and stirrups.
Design shear is checked at d from the support face, using τ_v against τ_c, and stirrups take only what concrete cannot.
Stirrups must be provided even when the concrete alone is strong enough, to hold the beam together and control crack width.
There is a hard ceiling τ_c,max; if τ_v crosses it, only a larger section works.
Torsion is handled by converting the torque into an equivalent shear and an equivalent moment, so the same shear and flexural design tools apply.
Bond is the only reason steel and concrete act together; without enough embedment the bar pulls out instead of yielding.
Development length depends on bar diameter and bar stress, not on the length of the beam or the size of the load.
Curtailment and splicing are where real beams fail: the moment diagram, the development length and the code's extension rules must all be satisfied at the cut.
bank_note: Long answers usually want both halves together — the behaviour (why diagonal cracks form, what bond really is) and the code procedure that follows from it (τ_v against τ_c and stirrup design, or V_e and M_t and the combined check) — so never write the steps without the reason behind them.

bank.q: Explain how a reinforced concrete beam without any shear reinforcement resists shear. Name each contribution and say which one is lost once a wide crack opens.
outline: Uncracked stage: shear stress τ = VQ/(Ib), principal tension at 45°
Crack forms when principal tensile stress exceeds concrete tensile strength
Compression zone above the crack carries shear
Aggregate interlock across crack faces
Dowel action of longitudinal bars crossing the crack
Stirrups, where present, act as the fourth mechanism
Aggregate interlock and dowel action drop sharply as crack width grows

bank.q: Define nominal shear stress and design shear strength of concrete. Explain why τ_v is compared with τ_c and what the designer must do if τ_v exceeds τ_c,max.
outline: τ_v = V_u/(b d), with terms defined and units
τ_c from the code table, function of grade of concrete and p_t = 100A_st/(b d)
Explain that τ_c is the concrete contribution, so the excess goes to stirrups
τ_c,max is the crushing limit of the diagonal strut
If τ_v > τ_c,max, redesign the section (increase b or D); more stirrups do not help

bank.q: Explain what bond is between reinforcing steel and concrete, where it comes from, and why a bar must be embedded a development length before it can carry its full force.
outline: Bond as shear at the steel–concrete interface
Sources: adhesion, friction, mechanical interlock of ribs
Flexural bond versus anchorage bond
τ_bd = F/(π φ L) derived from force balance
Setting τ_bd equal to the permissible value gives L_d = φ σ_s/(4 τ_bd)
L_d independent of the load, depends on bar diameter and stress
Consequence: a small bar needs a shorter embedment than a large one at the same stress

bank.q: State the code rules for lap length in tension and in compression, and explain why laps are staggered rather than bunched at one section.
outline: Lap length is at least the development length L_d
Longer minimum for direct tension than for flexural tension
Compression laps smaller than tension laps
Laps staggered so that a large fraction of the steel is not spliced at one section
Reason: a spliced section is weaker in bond and concentrates cracking
Small bars lap better than large bars; large bars need mechanical couplers or welding

bank.q: A simply supported beam of width 250 mm and effective depth 450 mm carries a factored shear of 150 kN at the support. Take f_ck = 25 N/mm², f_y = 415 N/mm², and tension steel of three 20 mm bars. Design the vertical stirrups and give the spacing layout along the span.
outline: Compute τ_v = V_u/(b d) and p_t = 100A_st/(b d)
Read τ_c and τ_c,max from the code tables and check the section
V_us = V_u − τ_c b d
Choose two-legged 8 mm stirrups, A_sv = 2 × 50.3 mm²
s_v = 0.87 f_y A_sv d / V_us
Check s_v against minimum shear reinforcement and against the maximum spacing limit
Vary spacing in zones from the shear force diagram; round down to a practical value
Sketch the layout with the first stirrup close to the support

bank.q: A beam of width 300 mm and overall depth 600 mm carries, at a section, a factored shear of 180 kN and a factored torque of 40 kN m. Compute the equivalent shear and equivalent moment and explain how the stirrups and longitudinal steel are then designed.
outline: V_e = V_u + 1.6 T_u/b with consistent units
Design stirrups for V_e using the usual shear route
Total longitudinal steel from M_u + M_t acting together
Check the section against the torsional shear limit
Provide side face reinforcement when the depth is large
Note that torsion steel must be closed links anchored properly

bank.q: Show, with numbers, how to check the development length at a simple support and decide whether a standard 90° bend is required.
outline: Bar force at the section from the bending moment
L_d = φ σ_s/(4 τ_bd) or the code value 0.87 f_y φ/(4 τ_bd)
Available embedment from the support face, counting cover and the anchorage value of the bend (8φ for 90°)
Compare and add a bend or increase the embedment if short
Mention that at least one third of the positive steel must reach the support

bank.q: The design gives V_us = 90 kN at a section of a beam with d = 500 mm, f_y = 415 N/mm², using two-legged 10 mm stirrups. Find the required spacing and verify the minimum shear reinforcement requirement.
outline: s_v = 0.87 f_y A_sv d / V_us
Compare with minimum A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y)
Compare with the maximum spacing limit related to d
State the adopted spacing and why it is rounded down

bank.q: Prepare a reinforcement detailing scheme for a rectangular beam carrying combined bending, shear and torsion, showing the stirrups, torsion links, longitudinal bars and cover.
outline: Closed stirrups anchored around the longitudinal bar
Spacing from shear design, and the extra torsional requirement
Longitudinal steel placed near the corners of the links
Side face reinforcement for deep webs
Nominal cover from the exposure class
Bar spacing rules for crack control and concreting
Section and side elevation drawing conventions

bank.q: IS 456 does not design a beam in torsion by torsional theory; it uses equivalent shear and equivalent moment. Explain why, and give two situations where this simplification can mislead the designer.
outline: True torsional stress distribution is complex and depends on compatibility
Equivalent shear and moment reduce torsion to familiar design tools
Result is conservative for ordinary beams
Where it is unsafe or inadequate: equilibrium torsion where the member must carry the torque for stability
Thin-walled or flanged members where the shear flow path differs
Interaction with bending at the section is not captured fully
Secondary effects such as crack width and serviceability need separate thought

bank.q: A contractor cuts off half of the bottom bars exactly where the bending moment diagram shows they are no longer needed. Analyse what can go wrong, and state what the code requires instead.
outline: Moment at the section is not the whole story: bond and shear interact
A bar must be developed before it carries its force, so the cut point moves towards midspan
Code requires the bar to extend beyond the theoretical cut-off by at least d or 12φ
Limits on how much steel may be curtailed or stopped at one section
Diagonal tension cracks shift the point of maximum bar force
Sudden loss of steel causes a brittle failure near the support region
Correct procedure: shift the moment diagram, then cut in steps

bank.q: Discuss how shear span-to-depth ratio, concrete grade and stirrup spacing change the mode of shear failure of a beam.
outline: Small shear span: arch action and diagonal compression, crushing type failure
Large shear span: beam action, diagonal tension failure
Very slender: flexural failure before shear
Higher concrete grade raises both τ_c and τ_c,max
Closer stirrups change brittle diagonal tension failure into a ductile, yielding mode
Minimum stirrups prevent sudden failure without shear reinforcement
Link to the code requirement of links at all sections

bank.q: Assess how far detailing — cover, spacing, anchorage and laps — decides the real safety of a beam. Use the interaction of bond and shear in your answer.
outline: Calculated steel cannot work without adequate cover and anchorage
Thin cover corrodes, low cover loses fire resistance
Crowded bars prevent concrete from reaching the steel
Bond and shear act together: diagonal cracks cut the embedment short
Anchorage at supports is where shear is highest
Poor laps behave like short development lengths and fail in pull-out
Detailing is design, not drafting

glossary.def: Distance from a point load to the nearer support; the shear span-to-depth ratio decides the type of shear failure.
Inclined crack that starts as a vertical flexural crack and bends over towards the load as shear stress opens it.
Inclined crack that forms in the web of a beam where the principal tensile stress is highest, often before flexural cracking.
Closed vertical or inclined link placed around the longitudinal bars to carry shear and to hold the cage together.
Longitudinal tension bar bent up near the support to act as inclined shear reinforcement.
Twisting action on a member, measured as a torque T about the longitudinal axis in N mm.
Torsion that is required for the member to stay in equilibrium, so it cannot be redistributed or reduced.
Torsion arising from the need to keep adjoining parts together, which may be reduced by cracking and redistribution.
Shear stress circulating around the section, added to the ordinary shear stress when a torque acts.
Steel placed along the two faces of a deep web, required when the overall depth exceeds the code value, to control cracking.
Transfer of force between a bar and the surrounding concrete by adhesion, friction and mechanical interlock.
Bond needed because the bending moment, and therefore the bar force, changes from section to section.
Bond needed to hold the ends of a bar so that its force is transferred to the concrete.
Additional hold given to a bar end by a bend, hook or plate beyond the straight embedment.
Curved end given to a bar to provide anchorage; a standard semicircular hook has an anchorage value of about 16φ.
Length over which two bars overlap to transfer force, never less than the development length.
Stopping some bars where the bending moment has fallen, subject to development and extension rules.
Moment diagram moved horizontally by the effective depth to account for diagonal tension when bars are curtailed.
Distance from the extreme compression fibre to the centroid of the tension steel, symbol d, in mm.
Actual distance from the concrete surface to the nearest steel surface measured on site.
Classification of the environment (mild, moderate, severe and so on) that fixes the minimum cover and concrete grade.
Value of strength below which not more than five per cent of test results are expected to fall; f_ck for concrete, f_y for steel.
Condition just before the structure fails, checked with factored loads and partial safety factors.
